subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
'Chetan? Sorry, can I ask something stupid?'
'Probably not stupid. Go on, Leela.'
'In the stand-up, what's a "blocker"? Everyone kept saying it.'
'Anything stopping your work. Like if you're waiting on someone else's code.'
'Oh. Okay.' Leela let out a breath and pushed her hair back. 'I thought everyone just knew these things.'
Chetan laughed. 'A year ago I sat exactly where you're sitting. I thought "sprint" meant we had to physically run somewhere.'
'You?'
'Me. And last week I didn't know what a "feature flag" was. Asked Anirudh. Still not sure I get it fully.' He shrugged. 'You don't stop not-knowing things here. You just stop being scared of it.'
Leela smiled. 'Can I keep asking you?'
'Please. Someone asked me a hundred questions my first month. It's my turn.' He pulled over a chair. 'Show me your first ticket. We'll do it together.'

qa.q: What does 'blocker' mean, according to Chetan?
qa.a: Anything stopping your work, like waiting on someone else's code.

qa.q: What does Leela's long breath suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests relief, since she had worried that everyone else already knew these things and she didn't.

qa.q: How does Chetan's attitude help both Leela and himself?
qa.a: He admits he still doesn't know everything and helps her openly, which makes her feel safe and deepens his own sense of belonging on the team.

qa.q: How might Leela see Chetan after hearing about 'sprint'?
qa.a: She may see him as approachable rather than intimidating, and feel her own confusion is normal.

grounding: It shows a person whose confidence has grown accepting that not knowing is normal and helping a newcomer, which strengthens his sense of belonging.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
It's odd. Eighteen months ago I was the one hiding in the staff room at the school, sure the principal had hired me by accident. Now I'm the one the new teachers are sent to.
This term it's Akash, twenty-three, straight from his B.Ed. On his second day he asked me, very quietly, how to fill in the attendance register, as if it were a secret. I laughed, kindly I hope, and told him I'd filled mine in wrong for the whole of my first month.
I don't know everything. Last week I had to ask the librarian how the new book-issue system works. I just ask now, without the old dread.
Helping Akash, I keep remembering my own first term, the chalk dust, the stomach aches. I feel fond of that version of me.
When he thanked me yesterday, I felt, for the first time, that I really belong here.
— Jahnavi

qa.q: What did Akash ask Jahnavi on his second day?
qa.a: He asked how to fill in the attendance register.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel now when remembering the first term?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels fond and a little nostalgic about that earlier, scared version of self.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's way of handling not knowing show about mature confidence?
qa.a: It shows that asking plainly, like asking the librarian, is normal, and that confidence can grow without pretending to know everything.

qa.q: How might Akash feel hearing that Jahnavi filled the register in wrong for a month?
qa.a: Akash may feel relieved and less ashamed, and more willing to ask further questions.

grounding: It shows a teacher whose confidence has grown with competence, who accepts not knowing everything and helps the next newcomer, cementing belonging.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Supervisor's note, customer insights team, end of quarter
I want to record a change in Nandini. A year ago she sat silently in our reviews and apologised for every question. This week she ran the onboarding for our new analyst, Arohi.
When Arohi asked what a retention curve was, Nandini said, "Honestly, I asked that exact question in my second week. Took me a month to really get it." Then she walked Arohi through one of her own old charts, including the mistake she had made on it.
Later, in the review, a director asked Nandini something she didn't know. She said, "I'm not sure; I'll check and come back by Friday," without any of the old panic.
Arohi told me at lunch that Nandini made her feel it was normal not to know yet. I'd like Nandini to be the buddy for the next two hires as well.

qa.q: What did Arohi ask Nandini about?
qa.a: What a retention curve was.

qa.q: How does Nandini seem to feel when she doesn't know the director's answer?
qa.a: She seems calm and secure, able to say she isn't sure without the old panic.

qa.q: What does the supervisor plan next, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Making Nandini the buddy for the next two hires, because helping newcomers strengthens her own belonging and helps them too.

qa.q: What is it like for Arohi to learn from Nandini?
qa.a: Arohi feels reassured and less alone, since Nandini admits her own early confusion and mistakes.

grounding: A supervisor notes a young analyst who now accepts not knowing everything and helps the next newcomer, deepening her belonging.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Sunday, 21 July
Rashmi started on our team on Monday, and every time she said "sorry, dumb question," I heard myself from two years ago. I used to keep a list of words to look up secretly in the washroom.
On Wednesday I took her for chai and told her the washroom story. She laughed so hard she spilled some on her kurta. Then I showed her my old notebook with "what is a sprint??" written on the first page, both question marks and all.
Funny thing: while explaining the release process to her, I got one step wrong, and she caught it from the manual. Two years ago that would have wrecked my week. Today I said, "Nice catch, you're right," and we fixed it together.
I don't know everything. I'm fine with that now. And being the person someone asks feels like more proof that I belong here than any appraisal did.
Amandeep

qa.q: What was written on the first page of the old notebook?
qa.a: What is a sprint??

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when Rashmi caught the mistake?
qa.a: Amandeep felt calm and even pleased, able to say 'nice catch' without the old panic.

qa.q: Why does helping Rashmi strengthen Amandeep's own sense of belonging?
qa.a: Being the one who explains and shares the old notebook shows Amandeep how far things have come, which feels like stronger proof than any appraisal.

qa.q: What is Rashmi's first week like after the chai?
qa.a: Rashmi feels relieved and more at ease, knowing a senior once felt just as lost 🙂

grounding: A young professional accepts not knowing everything and helps a newcomer, which confirms their own belonging.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: A year after joining the farm advisory office in Barabanki, Indu still didn't know every seed variety by name, and she no longer pretended to. When a farmer asked about a new pest on his okra, she said, "I'm not sure. Let me check with the district lab and come to your field on Thursday," and she did. On Monday a new trainee, Vijay, arrived: pressed shirt, anxious eyes, nodding at every term. At lunch under the neem tree, Indu shared her tiffin and said, "In my first month I thought 'soil health card' was some kind of ID. Nobody knows everything here. Ask me anything." Vijay laughed, surprised, and asked three questions in a row. Walking back, Indu realised she had answered two of them easily. She felt, quietly, that she belonged.

qa.q: What did Indu tell the farmer about the new pest?
qa.a: That she wasn't sure and would check with the district lab and come to his field on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Indu feel walking back after lunch?
qa.a: She felt quietly settled, a sense that she belonged, after answering two of Vijay's questions easily.

qa.q: Why does Indu's openness about not knowing help Vijay?
qa.a: Sharing her own early mistake makes not knowing feel normal, so Vijay can ask questions instead of nodding.

qa.q: What is lunch under the neem tree like for Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay arrives anxious but laughs in surprise and feels safe enough to ask three questions.

grounding: Shows a worker whose confidence has grown with competence, accepting not knowing everything and helping the next newcomer, which deepens belonging.
